<reason>Side B won decisively by grounding the debate in the inescapable arithmetic of caregiver scarcity and trapping Side A in a fatal contradiction regarding the level of staffing home care requires. When Side B pointed out that one-on-one home care is impossible at scale, Side A used Q1 to claim that 24/7 staffing was a strawman and that home care relies on part-time, coordinated visits. Side B immediately used its own Q1 to ask who helps a frail elder at 2:00 a.m. during the unstaffed hours, forcing Side A in Rebuttal 2 to pivot back to promising overnight aides and 24/7 support. Side B ruthlessly exposed this dilemma: either home care is part-time and leaves dangerous gaps (filled by unpaid relatives), or it demands continuous one-on-one staffing that drains scarce workers away from collective settings where one aide can support multiple elders. Side B also persuasively showed that Side A's strict "medical necessity" threshold turns residential communities into last-resort crisis wards rather than proactive, barrier-free social environments.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's sequence across [B2.2], [B3.1], and [B4.1]: after countering Side A's telehealth argument by noting that a camera "cannot lift someone off the bathroom floor at 2:00 a.m.," Side B used Side A's own pressure question ([A3.1], which insisted home care only required "part-time" support) to force Side A into contradicting itself in [A4.1] and [A4.4] by promising overnight aides and 24/7 home staffing.</best_rebuttal>
